messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] using the base argument in nodemix?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

In a previous question to the group in 2008 it was asked whether it is possible to delete specific pairings of node types in the nodemix procedure and the answer at that point seemed to be no. However, it seems like this might be possible now with the BASE argument for nodemix. Does anyone know if the BASE argument works this way, and, if so, how do you tell it to omit specific pairings. The Morris/Handcock/Hunter article in JOSS states:

The optional base argument is a vector of integers corresponding to the
pairings that should not be included. If base contains only negative integers, then these
integers correspond to the only pairings that should be included. By default (i.e., with
base = NULL or base = 0), all pairings are included.

However, I have not successfully been able to omit pairings so far. My code is:

orecon3_model <- ergm(orecon ~ edges +
                gwesp(0.5, fixed=TRUE) + gwdsp(0.5,fixed=TRUE)+ gwdegree(0.5, fixed=TRUE)+ nodemix('oregonagencycon', base=),
                MCMCsamplesize=1e+5, maxit = 7, burnin = 1e+5, verbose=TRUE,
                control=control.ergm(steplength = 0.25))
summary(orecon3_model)

I am hoping to omit about 6 of the possible pairings (there are six categories of node type and the network is undirected): pairs 1.1, 2.2, 2.4, 2.6, 5.6, 6.6

Thanks!
Jenine

To whom it may concern, 

We are currently implementing the statnet ergm package to analyze different anatomical and functional neural networks and find the results quite promising. To be able to compare things with, e.g. mere motif counting approach, it would be handy to include large motifs. The ergmuserterms package is, unfortunately, not quite self-explaning, so that we are wondering whether someone already generated a code for larger motifs, e.g. similar to the available triad census a quad census (with 4 nodes) or even larger sets.


Thanks in advance for your support.


Andreas Daffertshofer
Bernadette van Wijk

Hi Jenine.  The base argument does in fact work with nodemix.  This is  
a bit clunky, but it's not hard to do.  Take a look at this example:

  data(faux.mesa.high)
  summary(faux.mesa.high~nodemix("Race"))
mix.Race.Black.Black  mix.Race.Black.Hisp   mix.Race.Hisp.Hisp  
mix.Race.Black.NatAm
                    0                    8                    
53                   13
  mix.Race.Hisp.NatAm mix.Race.NatAm.NatAm mix.Race.Black.Other   
mix.Race.Hisp.Other
                   41                   46                     
0                    1
mix.Race.NatAm.Other mix.Race.Other.Other mix.Race.Black.White   
mix.Race.Hisp.White
                    0                    0                     
5                   22
mix.Race.NatAm.White mix.Race.Other.White mix.Race.White.White
                   10                    0                    4

Suppose I wanted to omit all pairings involving the "Other" category.   
Notice that in the summary above, there are 15 total positions in the  
vector and "Other" occurs in positions 7, 8, 9, 10, and 14.   
Therefore, I can make these positions the base and get rid of them:

  summary(faux.mesa.high~nodemix("Race", base=c(7,8,9,10,14)))
mix.Race.Black.Black  mix.Race.Black.Hisp   mix.Race.Hisp.Hisp  
mix.Race.Black.NatAm
                    0                    8                    
53                   13
  mix.Race.Hisp.NatAm mix.Race.NatAm.NatAm mix.Race.Black.White   
mix.Race.Hisp.White
                   41                   46                     
5                   22
mix.Race.NatAm.White mix.Race.White.White
                   10                    4


Hope this helps.
Dave

data(florentine)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I thought people here might be interested in this:

I created an R package that enables somewhat easier conversion between 
network objects of class 'network' and networks of class 'igraph', from 
the respective packages. It is called 'intergraph'. More information here:

http://brokeringclosure.wordpress.com/2010/08/25/from-igraph-to-network-and-back-again/

The package is still experimental. It may give warnings during some of 
the operations. This happens most often at places where I was not sure 
what is the best default behavior so decided to warn the user about the 
choices made (for example when not copying some network/edge/vertex 
attribute).

*If you try it out I'm very interested in your feedback!*

A related issue:

To be able to build upon the 'network' package reliably I had to patch 
it to add the package namespace. Package namespaces, as definined here

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Package-name-spaces

are a necessary standard for R packages nowadays. I remember discussing 
this issue with Mark when I was visiting Stats dep. at UW in autumn 2008.

*Please seriously consider adding namespaces to all 'statnet' packages.*

The procedure should be very straightforward. For the 'network' package 
you add a NAMESPACE file to the top level of package directory 
containing two lines:

useDynLib("network")
exportPattern("^[^\\.]")

This will export all the R functions defined in the package which names 
do not start with a dot (there are none as far as I remember) and 
register the C functions contained in the package.

The namespaced 'network' package passes R CMD check. Additionally I ran 
all the examples and tests in 'ergm' and some other 'statnet' packages 
to check if it doesn't break something by accident. Everything performed 
seamlessly.

Michal

Hi David.  I have to say, I can't see any basis for the referee's

derivative matrix (the Hessian) of the approximated log-likelihood  
function -- they are the square roots of the diagonal of the inverse  
of the negative Hessian, to be exact -- and thus it's not clear to me  
how small standard errors (i.e., a very sharply peaked approximate  
likelihood surface at the maximum) might result from "poor  
convergence".  Perhaps someone else on the list can help with the  
intuition here, but it sounds to me as though (a) you have done all  
you could to try to rule out any convergence issues, and (b) there is  
no reason to suspect that low p-values are by themselves evidence of  
convergence issues.

Does this help?  (And does anyone else see something I'm missing?)

Dave

Hi, David -

David Schaefer wrote:
> Hi all,
>

> (in this case, p-values for all effect but one fell below .001).
> When estimating those models, the MCMC diagnostic plots showed no
> signs of degeneracy and the gof plots indicated the model reproduced
> the network well.  To be safe, I reran the models and increased the
> burnin to 10 million, the MCMC sample size to 200,000 and the
> sampling interval to 10,000.  The results don't change; the
> significance levels are just as extreme; and, the MCMC diagnostic
> plots look even better than before.
> 
> Is convergence something that I should be worried about?  If so, is
> there anything else I can do to check for it?  I should mention I am
> using ergm 2.2-4 and R 2.10.1.  I have included the model estimation
> command below.

I have seen that problem before (pseudo-convergence leading to strange 
standard error estimates), usually on large networks with models that 
had substantial dependence.  The fact that something can go wrong does 
not, however, necessarily imply that it has.  If, in this case, (1) the 
chain seems to be mixing well, (2) diagnostics look good, (3) your mean 
stats match closely match the observed statistics, and (4) you get 
consistent results with multiple runs, and (5) you have no particular 
reason to expect that something is amiss, then (given the length of the 
chains) it would seem that you are about as safe as you are likely to 
get.  Getting similar results for the covariate effects with the 
dependence terms removed, assuming you do, would also help rule out some 
sources of algorithmic malfeasance.

Did the reviewer suggest some specific reason to doubt the results?  If 
not, it isn't obvious to me why one would suggest this as a problem.  I 
have on occasion raised similar questions in reviews, but always because 
there was something funny in the results (or in the description of the 
fitting procedure) that suggested poor convergence.  Convergence issues 
are certainly a risk with these sorts of models (and they can be hard to 
detect), but one wouldn't suspect non-convergence simply on the basis of 
low p-values.

This reviewer may or may not have had a good reason for raising this 
issue, but one should be aware that there is a lot of mythology 
surrounding ERGMs these days.  Your reviewer might be an expert, whose 
question arises from a problem they noticed in your analysis, or they 
might be someone who once saw an ERGM talk, and who is now applying 
something they hazily remember having heard during an excessively 
caffeinated exchange between persons whose own expertise consisted of 
having attended an afternoon workshop.  It is wise to respond diligently 
and respectfully to reviewer comments, while also entertaining the 
possibility that some of them do not arise from a position of competence.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

feels intimidated by writing two lines of pseudo-code to an extra file.

'intergraph' package. Given that 'network' and 'igraph' are two main 
packages providing data structures for networks ('graph' package 
following closely) it would be really neat to have a somewhat unified 
interface to the data in both packages. What I have in mind is something 
like 'DBI' package in the case of interfacing relational data bases. It 
defines generic functions for which packages 'RMySQL', 'RSQLite' and

Unfortunately, this is just one of the programming practices that the Statnet project has adopted that runs counter to the R environment that they chose to work within. I did not check it with the history of the R sources nor Statnet
packages, but it may very well be that when the first Statnet packages
were written the namespace mechanism was not yet part of R itself. My
own first R packages did not use namespaces either, I added them later.
As I wrote in my initial e-mail, the modification to the package is
really tiny and non-intrusive, it does not affect any other code within
that package nor in any other packages depending on it.

> (1) Statnet imposes an unusual modification on the semantics of
> formula objects in R. In no other R package does one write a formula
> in which complex object (i.e. the network, which contains many
> vectors of differing lengths) is expressed in terms of objects
> contained within it.
>
> (2) Insistence on C code (ostensibly for speed), to the point of
> incorporating legacy code that duplicates basic functionality of the
> BLAS in R (e.g. eigen decomposition). This actually flies in the face
> of the speed criterion, because the R BLAS is optimized for
> multiple-core architectures (not as common when the Statnet project
> started as they are now), and the legacy code is not (nor is
> specialized Statnet C code like the network layout code necessarily
> multi-processor optimized).

I do not really see any conflict nor interdependence between the the use
of namespaces and the first two issues you mentioned. The namespace
can be added to a package irrespectively whether the functions in that
package use formula objects in a non-standard way, duplicate some
functionality (whether written in R on in C) in base R or some other
packages etc. It is just a mechanism enabling the users to, among other
things, use a consistent way of calling functions with the same names
that come from different packages.

In fact, if you plan to duplicate a certain functionality, say an R
function, it may even make more sense to call the new function the same
way as the original to indicate that it is designed to do the same thing
and then use the namespace so that the users can choose to import the
version they prefer.

> (3) Statnet has dependencies on packages that bear a UW license
> which is NOT compatible with GPL licenses, meaning that Statnet and
> code that uses Statnet packages raise legal complications regarding
> licensing that are likely to surprise many users. Specifically, "for
> profit" uses of some parts of the code potentially require payment of
> royalty fees to UW (the GPL license of R has no such restriction).

Well, this seems to me as a completely different matter. Indeed, I am a
bit surprised with what you wrote. I just had a look at the sources of
'network' and 'ergm' (COPYING and LICENSE files) and they both seem to
be under GPL (?). Statnet authors, please clarify.

Taking the issue a bit more generally. There are other
packages in the R World created to work with network data, like 'igraph'
and 'graph'. Apart from the data structures for networks, they do
provide a lot of other functionality. I see that functionality
definitely *complementary* to all the things that were created within
Statnet. For me as a network modeling person it was always a real pain
going back and forth between 'igraph' and 'network' while, say, running
some community detection algorithm in 'igraph' and then fitting some
ERGMs to the same data set.

It is of course the decision of a package author whether, while writing
the package, he/she facilitates or impedes using his/her package
together with other R packages designed to work with the same type of data.

Nevertheless, whatever Statnet's standing about the licensing is, in my
opinion, it does not have much to do with the "technical" benefits of
having the packages NAMESPACEd.

> The above problems, like the namespace issue, make Statnet not play
> well with other packages, and for this reason any use of Statnet is
> awkward for me. It would be good if the Statnet team could give some
> attention to them, so that it can interoperate better with R and
> other R packages.

Two thumbs up about that. Although, as I wrote above, the other issues
(apart from namespaces) do not seem to be that "severe" for 
interoperability with other packages.

I think this is a really great endeavor, and am extremely happy to see
someone take this up. I have used igraph quite a bit, mostly because I have
been using very large networks. However, statnet and the network package
have a bunch of really useful functions available. Some get ported between
the two packages, but many do not. I have ended up writing some conversion
functions myself, but having them nicely encapsulated in an interface
package would be really great. For me personally, it would probably increase
my use of statnet quite a bit.

I'm too grateful both to the authors of statnet and igraph to fully endorse
the somewhat harsh tone of John's email, although all of his points seem
like things that could improve the attractiveness of statnet to a number of
audiences. As for licensing specifically, I've personally released stuff
under non-commercial-only license. I feel that the decision of license is a
very personal one, and that it is seldom reasonable to phrase requests for
changes in licensing in terms of 'should' (*).

However, as for using namespaces when writing public packages for R, I am
very close to using the 'should' word, and will second a hearty call to
'please please please' add namespaces to network and related packages.

In the end, we are all trying to help each other out in doing good research
and pushing forward the frontiers of knowledge (**). In this, increased
interoperability between the 'competing' packages helps everyone. However, I
am also very sensitive to the fact that although the open-source licenses
that most of the code is released under allow lots of changes by third
parties, it tends to be most productive to involve all authors/copyright
holder in a constructive relationship.

I look very much forward to seeing the outcome of the intergraph project,
which builds on two great packages.

Best,
Magnus

(*) Re-reading John's email, I see that it could be interpreted as
suggesting that the dependencies be removed, rather than the licenses being
changed. I don't know the code in question well enough to know if it would
be feasible to do so without loosing a lot of functionality, but if the
dependency was very minimal, that would seem like a good idea.

(**) All this talk about helping each other out reminded me that I have been
intending to respond to a request for help on this list for over a month now
:-P Hopefully, I'll be able to address that soon.

Hi, John -

John Paolillo wrote:
> The point about namespaces is well-made by Michal, but really it
> should have been obvious and best practice would have indicated using
> R namespaces at the outset of the Statnet project. 

This would have been rather difficult, since namespaces were unused 
and/or non-existent when the first bits of statnet were being assembled. 
   Back then, R had a very small community, and we dealt with conflicts 
via the time-honored method of not creating duplicate nomenclature (also 
called "not being a jerk," though circumstances have changed since 
then).  I don't recall when current the R NAMESPACE system first came 
into existence -- I suspect that it postdates sna -- but it was 
essentially unused until just a few years ago.  If the R precognition 
library had been available back then, perhaps we would have done things 
differently.  (Of course, seriously entertaining the idea that R would 
become so popular -- especially among network analysts -- that there 
might be a need for such a thing would have been grounds at that time 
for diagnosis of narcissistic personality disorder.)

If you are new to R, then you will doubtless be mystified by many things 
you find in the older packages.  These are the legacies of a wild, 
frontier age, when the documentation standards were loose, you could use 
generics any way you wanted, and the actual rules for R package 
construction were determined by a complex version of 20 questions. 
(This last is still true, to an extent.)  To those who have grown up 
with sidewalks and indoor plumbing, the free-wheeling designs of this 
earlier period doubtless carry a whiff of the barbaric.  As the heavy 
hand of civilization has descended upon the R community (with an influx 
of new users and developers unencumbered by history), however, many of 
our packages have gradually been subjugated to the useful and the good. 
  Thus are the fruits of the ancient days of R made available to its 
modern, enlightened user base, though they must occasionally cope with 
the narrow streets, blind alleys, and poor sewage treatment that 
accompany legacy code.

> 
> (1) Statnet imposes an unusual modification on the semantics of
> formula objects in R. In no other R package does one write a formula
> in which complex object (i.e. the network, which contains many
> vectors of differing lengths) is expressed in terms of objects
> contained within it.

Why, thank you.  We like to stay ahead of the curve.

> 
> (2) Insistence on C code (ostensibly for speed), to the point of
> incorporating legacy code that duplicates basic functionality of the
> BLAS in R (e.g. eigen decomposition). This actually flies in the face
> of the speed criterion, because the R BLAS is optimized for
> multiple-core architectures (not as common when the Statnet project
> started as they are now), and the legacy code is not (nor is
> specialized Statnet C code like the network layout code necessarily
> multi-processor optimized).

Ah yes, the good ole' days, before C backending.  Back then, you could 
almost compute betweenness on a 100 node network, if your life 
expectancy was high enough.  (But then, you didn't have data sets that 
big, so this was not so horrid as might be imagined.)  You will find 
that nearly everything in some packages is now backended, and none of it 
for the pure joy of writing in C.  If something is backended, there is 
usually a good reason for it -- generally, that reason being that the 
requisite R builtins were non-existent, slow, inapplicable, non-robust, 
etc.  As R evolves, it may gradually become possible to shift from using 
custom backends to R internal functions, and I expect that such things 
will occur.  (Of course, one does not tamper with working code unless 
one has a very good reason to do so, so there would need to be clear 
evidence of performance gains.)

With respect to your specific question re:BLAS, I'm not sure to what 
code you are referring.  I can, however, provide an illustrative case 
study (for those who are curious about how the process works).  A few 
releases ago, I switched the default method for evcent from the standard 
R eigen() method to a customized internal version, since I was able to 
obtain substantial memory and performance improvements on large graphs 
by so doing, and since I had received some requests in that regard.  The 
custom backend generally performs much better for this specific task, 
but is less robust than the backend that R uses; for that reason, and 
for compatibility with legacy code, the option to use the R built-in was 
included.  I certainly wouldn't have bothered with creating a custom 
backend if it wasn't needed, having better things to do with my scarce 
time than reinvent a somewhat lumpy wheel.  In this case, however, there 
was a need, the code resolved that need, and the change was worth 
making.  If you have better backend code that you would like to 
contribute, please feel free -- there is a whole laundry list of things 
in there that could stand to be improved.

> 
> (3) Statnet has dependencies on packages that bear a UW license which
> is NOT compatible with GPL licenses, meaning that Statnet and code
> that uses Statnet packages raise legal complications regarding
> licensing that are likely to surprise many users. Specifically, "for
> profit" uses of some parts of the code potentially require payment of
> royalty fees to UW (the GPL license of R has no such restriction).
> 

As far as I know, there is one optional package (latentnet) that has one 
such dependency on an external R package with a possibly funny license 
(mclust).  The statnet public releases are all GPL (v2 or v3, 
depending), and the core packages have no such dependencies AFAIK. 
Perhaps you would like to expand on the list of "packages" involved? 
(Or, by "dependencies" and "packages," did you mean "dependency" and 
"package?")  I would also be interested to learn what parts of the 
statnet code require payment of royalty fees to UW.  Perhaps this was 
decided at a super-secret meeting to which I wasn't invited.

> The above problems, like the namespace issue, make Statnet not play
> well with other packages, and for this reason any use of Statnet is
> awkward for me. It would be good if the Statnet team could give some
> attention to them, so that it can interoperate better with R and
> other R packages.

Despite all evidence to the contrary, we do love our peeps, and we try 
to evolve our toolkit in response to user input.  This is more like 
steering a tanker than a motorboat, so the salutary effects of 
belligerence are not always immediate; and, of course, there are some 
cases in which well-intentioned suggestions are unwise or infeasible due 
to engineering trade-offs that are not apparent to the person making the 
suggestion.  The R world has changed radically over the past few years, 
as have the kind of data analysis challenges that we and our peers face. 
  (When I wrote the first version of sna, the largest complete network 
data set of which I was aware had about 60 nodes.)  In the face of such 
challenges, our ragtag band of sociologists, anthropologists, and 
statisticians attempts to provide the best free software reasonably 
producible by amateur developers working in their spare time.  So long 
as we and others find it useful, we will continue to do so.

Thanks,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michal -

Michal Bojanowski wrote:
> I can understand why S4 is considered by some people an over(haul/kill). 
> But as far as it goes for namespaces: they are very practical, 
> especially in case of multiple name conflicts, like between 'network' 
> and 'igraph'. I do think namespaces will be more and more indispensable 
> given the pace at which the number of packages available through CRAN 
> grows. I also believe that adding namespaces will make extending 
> 'network' and Statnet much easier. Simultaneously, I do not really see 
> any harmful side effects of using namespaces, unless of course somebody 
> feels intimidated by writing two lines of pseudo-code to an extra file.

It is always possible that I am exaggerating my opposition for purposes 
of humorous effect and/or to distract the reader from considering 
accusations of sloth on my part, though I prefer to let such questions 
remain in the domain of personal speculation.  From an end user 
perspective, the main downside of namespaces is that they reduce the 
transparency of access to code within the interpreter (since you need to 
know what namespace the function is in, and query it correctly).  This 
is not terribly difficult, but is IMHO a lot less obvious for new users 
(and I find it a pain, myself).  From a developer's point of view, the 
only real concern is making sure that there's not some highly 
non-obvious bug in cross-package compatibility that will suddenly arise 
when you add namespaces to your package.  That may seem unlikely, but 
maintaining multiple interdependent packages teaches one the Tao of 
Paranoia.

 From a historical perspective, collision problems used to be avoided by 
not creating packages with duplicate nomenclature.  That was eminently 
doable, even until very recently.  But the R world has changed, the 
number of packages has grown to the point where collisions are a real 
issue, and needs of the network community have become sufficiently 
diverse that multiple R-based toolkits start to make sense.  In this 
environment, I am persuaded that namespaces are a regrettable necessity. 
  (There is still no excuse for American Idol.)

> 
> To be honest I have somewhat farther-reaching plans as it goes for the 
> 'intergraph' package.
 >...
> I'm curious what you and other Statnet-ers would think about such a 
> project.

It's an interesting issue.  Back when we started building statnet per 
se, the idea was to build the network class as a unifying data 
structure.  It works pretty damn well (though it has legacy aspects that 
could be improved), but my sense at this stage is that the increasing 
scale and diversity of network data sets is such that no one structure 
is going to work well for all applications.  There are intrinsic 
engineering tradeoffs involved in choosing one representation over 
another, and nothing makes everyone happy.  As it is, I use adjacency 
matrices when just playing around with simple structures, network 
objects for large/complex networks with rich metadata, and sna edgelists 
for ultra-huge networks with ~1e6 nodes/edges.  (Actually, I've also 
used network objects for the latter, but even the linear costs of 
metadata support start to become a concern when you are squeezing every 
bit of RAM out of your machine.)  We also have projects that are 
starting to require database storage (as you describe), for incompletely 
observed networks of unthinkable size.  Trying to shoehorn all of this 
into one class would require a very special brand of madness.

Given that, the idea of working towards a unified API (or 
``meta-class,'' as it were) to form another abstraction layer between 
the usual class-level data representation and the analysis tools would 
seem to have promise.  Very difficult to do well, however.  In the short 
term, a more systematic scheme for class conversion would doubtless be 
helpful.  (Otherwise, our packages have to know how to decode everyone 
else's classes, which is not practical.  And vice versa.)  Not speaking 
for the other members of the team, I am sympathetic to supporting such a 
lingua franca effort if (1) it's well-designed, (2) doesn't break 
anything, and (3) doesn't create maintenance problems down the road.  I 
have learned the hard way to be very careful vis a vis (2) and (3), and 
do not lightly make changes to the network class.  But persuasion is not 
impossible, and I am open to specific proposals.

Cheers,

-Carter
